    Slide 4-6: Key Ideas about Sorting

    Visuals: * A list that builds up sequentially over 3 steps.

    Transcript: Key Ideas about Sorting

    1. Many quadratic (\(O(n^2)\)) sorting algorithms work fast on arrays of small size.
      • This happens due to efficient loops and use of processor cache. The RAM model that we use does not take this into account. The external memory (I/O) model does, but it is out of scope for this course.
    2. In general, sorting cannot be faster than \(\Omega(n \log n)\).
      • This is true for comparison-based sorts. We will prove this today.
    3. In special cases, sorting is possible in linear time (\(O(n)\))
      • There are several linear sorts, we will consider some of them today.

    4

    Slide 7: Section Header

    Visuals: * Title text centered.

    Transcript: Lower Bound for Sorting Algorithms

    Slide 8-28: Sorting Algorithms (review)

    Visuals: * This slide builds a comparison table of sorting algorithms step-by-step. * It lists Insertion sort, Selection sort, Merge sort, and Quicksort. * It fills in Worst-case, Best-case, and properties (In-place, stable) one by one.

    Final Transcript (summarizing the completed slide): Sorting Algorithms (review)

    1. Insertion sort:
      • Worst-case complexity: \(O(n^2)\)
      • Best-case complexity: \(O(n)\)
      • In-place, stable, works fast on small and nearly sorted arrays
    2. Selection sort
      • Worst-case complexity: \(O(n^2)\)
      • Best-case complexity: \(O(n^2)\)
      • In-place, stable, requires \(O(n)\) write operations
    3. Merge sort
      • Worst-case complexity: \(O(n \log n)\)
      • Best-case complexity: \(O(n \log n)\)
      • Not in-place (requires \(O(n)\) additional memory), stable
    4. Quicksort
      • Worst-case complexity: \(O(n^2)\)
      • Average-case complexity: \(O(n \log n)\)
      • In-place, stable, fast in practice

    Slide 29-33: Lower Bound for Sorting Algorithms (idea)

    Visuals: * Text explanation that builds up.

    Transcript: Lower Bound for Sorting Algorithms (idea)

    All algorithms we have seen so far: 1. use only the comparison operation (\(\le\)) to order elements, 2. work in \(\Omega(n \log n)\) in the worst case.

    Let us prove that this lower bound holds for any sorting algorithm that relies on the comparison operation to make decisions.

    We will rely on the decision tree formalism (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.1)

    6

    Slide 34-39: Decision Tree (idea)

    Visuals: * Text definitions describing a decision tree structure.

    Transcript: Decision Tree (idea)

    A decision tree is a binary tree: 1. Each node of the tree is either a leaf (no child nodes), or has exactly two child nodes. 2. Leaves correspond to a possible outcome of the algorithm (sorting result). 3. Internal nodes correspond to making a decision based on one comparison (one operation of the form \(A[i] \le A[j]\)).

    For any algorithm and any input size, we can construct a decision tree.

    Each path from the root to a leaf corresponds to a possible execution path of the algorithm.

    7

    Slide 40: Decision Tree Model (Example)

    Visuals: * A diagram of a decision tree for insertion sort of three elements \(\langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle\). * Root Node: “1:2” (Compare index 1 and 2). * Left Branch (\(\le\)): Goes to Node “2:3”. * Left Branch (\(\le\)): Leaf \(\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle\). * Right Branch (\(>\)): Goes to Node “1:3”. * Left Branch (\(\le\)): Leaf \(\langle 1, 3, 2 \rangle\). * Right Branch (\(>\)): Leaf \(\langle 3, 1, 2 \rangle\). * Right Branch (\(>\)): Goes to Node “1:3” (from root). * …and so on, showing permutations like \(\langle 2, 1, 3 \rangle\), \(\langle 2, 3, 1 \rangle\), etc. * Handwritten Annotation: Top left: “Input \(\langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle\)”. Top right: “At least \(n!\) leaves”. A red circle highlights the root node “1:2”. Orange highlights trace a specific path through the tree. Underlines specific leaves.

    Transcript: Decision Tree Model (insertion sort for three elements)

    [Figure 1: Decision tree for insertion sort of three elements (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.1).]

    Slide 41: Handwritten Logic (Insertion Sort Trace)

    Visuals: * A completely handwritten slide illustrating the logic of insertion sort comparisons. * Top left: Array [a1 | a2 | a3]. * Tree Diagram: * Root: \(a_1 \le a_2\). * Left Child (\(\le\)): Comparison \(a_2 \le a_3\). * Left (\(\le\)): Outcome \(a_1 \le a_2 \le a_3\). * Right (\(>\)): Comparison \(a_1 \le a_3\). * Left (\(\le\)): Outcome \(a_1 \le a_3 \le a_2\). * Right (\(>\)): Outcome \(a_3 \le a_1 \le a_2\). * Right Child (\(>\)): Logic for when \(a_1 > a_2\), leading to comparison \(a_1 \le a_3\), etc. * Bottom: A generalized linear chain of comparisons \(a_1 \le a_2\), then \(a_2 \le a_3\), …, \(a_{n-1} \le a_n\).

    Transcript: [Transcribed Handwritten Text] \(a_1 \mid a_2 \mid a_3\)

    (Tree logic tracing comparisons:) Root: \(a_1 \le a_2\) If \(\le\): check \(a_2 \le a_3\) If \(\le\): order is \(a_1 \le a_2 \le a_3\) If \(>\): check \(a_1 \le a_3\) If \(\le\): order is \(a_1 \le a_3 \le a_2\) If \(>\): order is \(a_3 \le a_1 \le a_2\)

    If \(>\) (at root): check \(a_1 \le a_3\) … (logic continues for right branch)

    (Bottom Diagram shows linear dependency) \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\) Comparison chain: \(a_1 \le a_2 \rightarrow a_2 \le a_3 \dots \rightarrow a_{n-1} \le a_n\) Result: \(a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n\)

    Slide 42: Exercise 4.1 (Selection Sort)

Construct a decision tree for selection sort for an array of four elements.” * Handwriting: * Draws array [a1, a2, a3, a4]. * Writes pseudocode for Selection Sort: for i=n downto 2, m=1, for j=2 to i, if A[j] > A[m] then m=j. * Draws a partial decision tree. * Root: comparison 2:1. * Next level: 3:1 or 3:2. * Next level: 4:1 etc. * Shows the depth calculation: \(2^6 = 64\).

    Transcript: Decision Tree Model (selection sort)

    Exercise 4.1 Construct a decision tree for selection sort for an array of four elements.

    selection-sort(A, n): for \(i = n\) downto 2 \(m = 1\) for \(j = 2\) to \(i\) if not (\(A[j] \le A[m]\)) \(m = j\) exchange \(A[m]\) with \(A[i]\)

    Calculation at bottom: \(2^6 = 64\)

    Node: \(3:4\) (\(\le\)) Node: \(1:3\) (\(\le\)) Node: \(2:3\) (\(\le\)) or (\(>\)) Node: \(2:4\) Outcomes: \(\langle 1, 2, 3, 4 \rangle\), \(\langle 1, 3, 2, 4 \rangle\), \(\langle 1, 3, 4, 2 \rangle\)

    Slide 44-58: Lower Bound for Sorting (worst case)

    Visuals: * A slide that progressively adds mathematical text to prove the lower bound. * It introduces properties of decision trees and derives the formula. * Slide 46 includes handwritten diagrams of binary trees to illustrate height vs. leaves (\(h=1 \rightarrow 2\) leaves, \(h=3 \rightarrow 2^3=8\) leaves).

    Transcript: Lower Bound for Sorting (worst case)

    Note the following properties of decision trees for the sorting algorithms we have considered: 1. A decision tree always has at least \(n!\) leaves. 2. A complete binary tree of height \(h\) cannot have more than \(2^h\) leaves. * [Handwritten sketch on Slide 46]: Tree with \(h=1\) has 2 leaves. Tree with \(h=3\) has \(2^3=8\) leaves. 3. The worst case corresponds to the longest path from the root to a leaf.

    The lower bound on the running time of any sorting algorithm on an array of size \(n\) corresponds to the lower bound on the height of any decision tree for that array:

    \(2^h \ge n! \implies h \ge \log_2(n!)\)

    \(h \ge \log_2(n!)\) \(= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(i)\) \(= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(i) \ge \sum_{i=1}^{n/2} \log(i) + \sum_{i=n/2}^{n} \log(i)\) \(\ge \sum_{i=n/2}^{n} \log(i)\) \(\ge \sum_{i=n/2}^{n} \log(n/2)\) \(= \frac{n}{2} \log(\frac{n}{2})\) \(= \boxed{\Omega(n \log n)}\)

    Slide 62-66: Counting Sort (idea)

    Visuals: * Text explanation of the algorithm. * Slide 66 adds a purple puzzle piece icon with a question.

    Transcript: Counting Sort (idea)

    The idea of counting sort: 1. Assumption: the values to be sorted are in a small range of possible values (by default — numbers in the range from \(0\) to \(k - 1\), for some parameter \(k\)). 2. Instead of comparing elements, count the number of elements with each value: how many zeros, ones, twos, etc. are in the array. 3. Then write the numbers to the output array in the correct order, based on the count for each value.

    [Puzzle Icon] What real world data can be sorted using counting sort?

    14

    Slide 67-80: Counting Sort (naive variant)

    Visuals: * Input Array (Indices 1-8): [2, 5, 3, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3] * Animation Sequence: 1. Shows the input array. 2. Shows a Count Array (indices 0-5) initialized to empty/zeros. 3. Iterates through the input array: * Reads 2 -> increments index 2 in Count Array. * Reads 5 -> increments index 5. * Reads 3 -> increments index 3. * …and so on. 4. Final Count Array: 0:2, 1:0, 2:2, 3:3, 4:0, 5:1. 5. Reconstruction: Uses the Count Array to fill a new output array. * See 0 has count 2 -> writes 0, 0. * See 1 has count 0 -> writes nothing. * See 2 has count 2 -> writes 2, 2. * See 3 has count 3 -> writes 3, 3, 3. * See 5 has count 1 -> writes 5. * Slide 79/80: Adds text “Is this sort stable?” and “What about data that is not part of the key?”

    Transcript: Counting Sort (naive variant)

    [Visual demonstration of sorting the array: 2, 5, 3, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3] [Resulting Output: 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5]

    [Puzzle Icon] Is this sort stable? [Puzzle Icon] What about data that is not part of the key?

    15

    Slide 81-82: Counting Sort (instability)

    Visuals: * Shows the same input array but with associated data (letters) attached to the numbers to demonstrate stability. * Input: (2,a), (5,b), (3,c), (0,d), (2,e), (3,f), (0,g), (3,h). * Process: * The naive count puts all 0s first, then 2s, etc. * When reconstructing 0s, it puts 0 count=2. It places 0 and 0. However, the visual lines show that (0,d) and (0,g) might be swapped or lost if we just overwrite the array based on counts. * Result: The slide shows the output (0,?), (0,?), (2,?), ... indicating that the association with the original ‘a’, ‘b’, ‘c’ data is lost or the order is not guaranteed. * Slide 82 Text: “Do we have enough data to restore stability?”

    Transcript: Counting Sort (instability)

    [Diagram showing input pairs (Key, Value)] Input: (2,a), (5,b), (3,c), (0,d), (2,e), (3,f), (0,g), (3,h) [Diagram shows mapping to counts and naive reconstruction losing the link to values or order]

    [Puzzle Icon] Do we have enough data to restore stability?

    16

    Slide 83-103: Counting Sort (full variant)

    Visuals: * Demonstrates the Stable Counting Sort algorithm. * Input: (2,a), (5,b), (3,c), (0,d), (2,e), (3,f), (0,g), (3,h). * Step 1: Frequency Count: 0:2, 1:0, 2:2, 3:3, 4:0, 5:1. * Step 2: Cumulative Count: Modifies count array to show starting positions (or ending positions). * 0 count becomes 2. * 1 count becomes 2 (2+0). * 2 count becomes 4 (2+2). * 3 count becomes 7 (4+3). * 4 count becomes 7. * 5 count becomes 8. * Step 3: Placement (Backwards traversal): * Takes last element (3,h). Look at index 3 in count array. Value is 8. Place (3,h) at index 8. Decrement count to 7. * Takes (0,g). Look at index 0. Value is 2. Place (0,g) at index 2. Decrement count to 1. * Takes (3,f). Index 3 has count 7 (from before). Place (3,f) at index 7. Decrement to 6. * …Continues until done. * Slide 103 Text: “What ensures stability?”

    Transcript: Counting Sort (full variant)

    [Visual demonstration of Stable Counting Sort] 1. Count frequencies. 2. Calculate cumulative counts (prefix sums) to determine positions. 3. Traverse input array backwards, placing elements into the output array based on cumulative counts and decrementing the count.

    [Resulting Output is sorted and stable: (0,d), (0,g), (2,a), (2,e), (3,c), (3,f), (3,h), (5,b)]

    [Puzzle Icon] Is this sort stable? [Puzzle Icon] What ensures stability?

    17 & 18

    Slide 104-105: Counting Sort (pseudocode)

    Visuals: * Image: Figure 2: Pseudocode for counting sort (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.2). * Code: text COUNTING-SORT(A, n, k) 1 let B[1 : n] and C[0 : k] be new arrays 2 for i = 0 to k 3 C[i] = 0 4 for j = 1 to n 5 C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] + 1 6 // C[i] now contains the number of elements equal to i. 7 for i = 1 to k 8 C[i] = C[i] + C[i - 1] 9 // C[i] now contains the number of elements less than or equal to i. 10 // Copy A to B, starting from the end of A. 11 for j = n downto 1 12 B[C[A[j]]] = A[j] 13 C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] - 1 // to handle duplicate values 14 return B * Handwritten Annotations: * Next to lines 2-3: \(\Theta(k)\) * Next to lines 4-5: \(\Theta(n)\) * Next to lines 7-8: \(\Theta(k)\) * Next to lines 11-13: \(\Theta(n)\) * Grouping the whole block: \(\Theta(n+k)\) * Arrows pointing to the logic in line 12/13 labeling parts as A[j] - key and explaining C[A[j]] is “where to put A[j]”. * Slide 105: Adds puzzle text “What is the time and space complexity of counting sort?”

    Transcript: Counting Sort (pseudocode)

    COUNTING-SORT(A, n, k) 1 let \(B[1 : n]\) and \(C[0 : k]\) be new arrays 2 for \(i = 0\) to \(k\) 3 \(C[i] = 0\) 4 for \(j = 1\) to \(n\) 5 \(C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] + 1\) 6 // \(C[i]\) now contains the number of elements equal to \(i\). 7 for \(i = 1\) to \(k\) 8 \(C[i] = C[i] + C[i - 1]\) 9 // \(C[i]\) now contains the number of elements less than or equal to \(i\). 10 // Copy \(A\) to \(B\), starting from the end of \(A\). 11 for \(j = n\) downto \(1\) 12 \(B[C[A[j]]] = A[j]\) 13 \(C[A[j]] = C[A[j]] - 1\) // to handle duplicate values 14 return \(B\)

    Figure 2: Pseudocode for counting sort (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.2).

    \(\Theta(n)\) for counting. \(\Theta(k)\) for prefix sums. \(\Theta(n)\) for placement. Total: \(\Theta(n+k)\).

    [Puzzle Icon] What is the time and space complexity of counting sort?

    19

    Slide 106-110: Counting Sort (time complexity analysis)

    Visuals: * Text list analysis appearing step-by-step.

    Transcript: Counting Sort (time complexity analysis)

    The time complexity of counting sort: 1. Counting elements — \(\Theta(n)\). 2. Computing auxiliary indices — \(\Theta(k)\). 3. Filling the output array — \(\Theta(n)\).

    In total, the time complexity of counting sort is \(\boxed{\Theta(n + k)}\).

    Slide 115-121: Radix Sort (idea)

    Visuals: * Text steps appearing one by one.

    Transcript: Radix Sort (idea)

    The idea of radix sort: 1. Assumption: the values to be sorted are numbers consisting of \(d\) digits, where each digit can have values from \(0\) to \(k - 1\). 2. Sort the numbers by the first (least significant) digit. 3. Sort the numbers by the second digit. 4. … 5. Sort the numbers by the most significant digit. 6. The array is sorted!

    22

    Slide 122-133: Radix Sort (example)

    Visuals: * Array: [329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355] * Parameters (Handwritten): \(n=7\), \(d=3\), \(k=10\). * Animation Sequence: 1. Sort by last digit (Ones): Highlights 9, 7, 7, 9, 6, 0, 5. Reorders array based on these. * Result: 720, 355, 436, 457, 657, 329, 839 (Note: 457 comes before 657 because it was before it originally - stability). 2. Sort by middle digit (Tens): Highlights 2, 5, 3, 5, 5, 2, 3. Reorders. * Result: 720, 329, 436, 839, 355, 457, 657. 3. Sort by first digit (Hundreds): Highlights 7, 3, 4, 8, 3, 4, 6. Reorders. * Result: 329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839. Sorted. * Slide 132 (Handwritten Logic): Shows a tree-like breakdown of why sorting from least significant works. * Example numbers: 16, 36, 34, 52. * Sort by 1st (ones): 52, 34, 16, 36. * Sort by 2nd (tens): 16, 34, 36, 52. * Slide 133: Puzzle icon “Is this sort stable?”.

    The complexity of radix sort depends on the sorting algorithm used for digits: 1. with insertion sort for digits — \(O(d n^2)\) 2. with counting sort — \(\boxed{\Theta(d(n + k))}\)

    Slide 139: Radix Sort (complexity analysis, for numbers)

    Visuals: * Exercise 4.5: “Show that we can sort \(n\) \(d\)-bit numbers… in \(\Theta(d/r (n + 2^r))\)”. * Handwritten Derivation: * \(r=1 \implies \Theta(dn)\). * \(r=\log_2 d \implies \Theta(\frac{d}{\log_2 d}(n+d))\). * \(r=d \implies \Theta(n + 2^d)\). * Diagram of bits split into chunks of size \(r\). * Optimal \(r \approx \log n\). * Final complexity shown as \(\Theta(d \cdot (n+2^r)/r)\). Note: The slide has a box formula \(\Theta(d(n+2^r)/r)\).

    Transcript: Radix Sort (complexity analysis, for numbers)

    Exercise 4.5 Show that we can sort \(n\) \(d\)-bit numbers (i.e., numbers in binary representation) in \(\Theta \left( \frac{d}{r} (n + 2^r) \right)\) for any parameter \(1 \le r \le d\).

    \(r=\log_2 d \implies \Theta(\dots)\) \(r=d \implies \Theta(n+2^d)\) Shows bit array split into chunks of size \(k=2^r\) (values range). Complexity \(\Theta(d/r \cdot (n + 2^r))\).

    Slide 140: Section Header

    Visuals: * Title text centered.

    Transcript: Bucket Sort

    Slide 141-146: Bucket Sort (idea)

    Visuals: * Text steps appearing one by one. * Diagram of a number line split into intervals \([0, 1)\). * Handwritten note: “w. comparison-based sorting” (indicating how buckets are sorted).

    Transcript: Bucket Sort (idea)

    The idea of bucket sort: 1. Assumption: the values to be sorted are numbers, uniformly distributed in some range (by default — in the interval \([0, 1)\)), and a cheap rounding operation is available. 2. Divide the range of possible values into \(n\) equal\(^1\) intervals. 3. Add each value to the bucket corresponding to its interval (by rounding). 4. Sort the values in each bucket. [Handwritten arrow]: w. comparison-based sorting 5. Concatenate the sorted buckets.

    \(^1\) in probability

    27

    Slide 147-149: Bucket Sort (example)

    Visuals: * Image: Figure 4: Example of bucket sort (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.4). * Array A (size 10): .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, .68. * Array B (Buckets 0-9): * Bucket 1: .12 \rightarrow .17 * Bucket 2: .21 \rightarrow .23 \rightarrow .26 * Bucket 3: .39 * …etc. * Handwritten Note: Highlights Bucket 2. Writes “0.2 \(\le x <\) 0.3”. * Slide 149: Puzzle icons “Is bucket sort stable?” “Why do we choose \(n\) buckets?”.

    Transcript: Bucket Sort (example)

    [Figure 4: Shows Array A mapping values to linked lists in Array B (buckets).] [Handwritten annotation]: Range for bucket 2 is \(0.2 \le x < 0.3\).

    Figure 4: Example of bucket sort (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.4).

    [Puzzle Icon] Is bucket sort stable? [Puzzle Icon] Why do we choose \(n\) buckets?

    Slide 150-151: Bucket Sort (pseudocode)

    Visuals: * Image: Figure 5: Pseudocode for bucket sort. * Code: text BUCKET-SORT(A, n) 1 let B[0 : n - 1] be a new array 2 for i = 0 to n - 1 3 make B[i] an empty list 4 for i = 1 to n 5 insert A[i] into list B[ floor(n * A[i]) ] 6 for i = 0 to n - 1 7 sort list B[i] with insertion sort 8 concatenate the lists B[0], B[1], ..., B[n-1] together in order 9 return the concatenated lists * Handwritten Annotations: * Lines 2-3: \(\Theta(n)\) * Lines 4-5: \(\Theta(n)\) * Line 6: \(\Theta(n^2)\) (worst case) * Line 8: \(\Theta(n)\) * Formula floor(n * A[i]) is highlighted with arrow. * Slide 151: Puzzle icon “What is the complexity of bucket sort?”.

    Transcript: Bucket Sort (pseudocode)

    BUCKET-SORT(A, n) 1 let \(B[0 : n - 1]\) be a new array 2 for \(i = 0\) to \(n - 1\) 3 make \(B[i]\) an empty list 4 for \(i = 1\) to \(n\) 5 insert \(A[i]\) into list \(B[\lfloor n \cdot A[i] \rfloor]\) 6 for \(i = 0\) to \(n - 1\) 7 sort list \(B[i]\) with insertion sort 8 concatenate the lists \(B[0], B[1], \dots, B[n - 1]\) together in order 9 return the concatenated lists

    Figure 5: Pseudocode for bucket sort (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.4).

    Insertion sort step is \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst case. Formula for index: \(\lfloor n \cdot A[i] \rfloor\).

    [Puzzle Icon] What is the complexity of bucket sort?

    29

    Slide 152-160: Bucket Sort (complexity analysis)

    Visuals: * Text analysis steps.

    Transcript: Bucket Sort (complexity analysis)

    The complexity of bucket sort depends on the sorting algorithm used for buckets: 1. Initialization of \(n\) buckets — \(\Theta(n)\). 2. Filling buckets — \(\Theta(n)\). 3. Sorting buckets * with insertion sort — \(\Theta(n^2)\) in the worst case, but \(\Theta(n)\) on average! 4. Concatenation of buckets — \(\Theta(n)\).

    [Puzzle Icon] Intuitively, why is the average-case complexity of bucket sort \(\Theta(n)\)?

    30

    Slide 161: Bucket Sort (average-case complexity analysis)

    Visuals: * Mathematical derivation.

    Transcript: Bucket Sort (average-case complexity analysis)

    Let \(n_i\) be the size of the \(i\)-th bucket. Then the running time of bucket sort: \(T(n) = \Theta(n) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} O(n_i^2)\)

    The expected running time: \(E[T(n)] = E[\Theta(n)] + E \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} O(n_i^2) \right]\) \(= \Theta(n) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} E [O(n_i^2)]\)

    The expected time to sort each bucket is \(O(2 - \frac{1}{n})\), therefore the expected time complexity of bucket sort is \(\boxed{\Theta(n)}\). For the full proof, see (Cormen et al. 2022, §8.4).

    Visuals: * List of exercises 4.6 to 4.9. * Handwritten Notes: * Next to 4.6: “Counting Sort - \(\Theta(n + k)\)” and something looking like \(\Theta(n^5) = \Theta(n^5)\). * Next to 4.7: “Radix-Sort - \(\Theta(d(n+k)) = ?\)”. “\(n=10\), \(k=10^5\)”. * Slide 164 contains a table/calculation related to Exercise 4.7 (sorting numbers up to \(n^5\)). * \(0 \dots n^5-1\). \(d=5\), \(k=n\). \(\Theta(d(n+k)) = \Theta(5(n+n)) = \Theta(n)\). * Shows examples: \(n=10 \rightarrow 10^5-1\), \(n=100 \rightarrow 100^5-1\), etc. * Slide 165 contains a calculation for Exercise 4.6 (Range queries). * Array 0 3 0 1 0 0 1 3. * Count array 0:4, 1:2, 2:0, 3:2. * Prefix sums 0:4, 1:6, 2:6, 3:8. * Query example: How many \(x\) s.t. \(\lfloor 1.5 \rfloor < x \le \min(\lfloor 4.7 \rfloor, 3)\)? * Formula: Count(b) - Count(a-1) e.g., \(8 - 6 = 2\).

    Transcript: Exercises

    Exercise 4.6 Describe an algorithm that can process \(n\) numbers in the range from \(0\) to \(k\) so that any query of the form “how many elements in the array are in the range from \(a\) to \(b\)?” can be answered in \(\Theta(1)\). [Handwritten Solution]: Use Counting Sort prefix sums array. Range \([a, b]\) count is \(C[b] - C[a-1]\).

    Exercise 4.7 Propose an algorithm that sorts numbers in the range from \(0\) to \(n^5 - 1\) in \(\Theta(n)\). [Handwritten Solution]: Use Radix Sort with base \(k=n\). Number of digits \(d=5\). Complexity \(\Theta(d(n+k)) = \Theta(5(2n)) = \Theta(n)\).

    Exercise 4.8 Propose a way to improve the worst-case running time of Bucket-Sort to \(\Theta(n \log n)\). Can we improve the running time of Bucket-Sort to \(o(n \log n)\)?

    Exercise 4.9 Propose a way to improve the worst-case running time of Bucket-Sort.

    Problem Content: * Tab Menu: ЗАДАЧИ | ОТОСЛАТЬ | МОИ ПОСЫЛКИ | ЗАРЕГИСТРИРОВАННЫЕ УЧАСТНИКИ | ЗАПУСК * Title: A. The Magical Donut * Constraints: * time limit per test: 1 second * memory limit per test: 256 megabytes

    • Description:
      • Natasha prepared a big donut where the inner radius is \(R_1\) and the outer radius is \(R_2\), such that both circles are concentric and the origin is located at the center.
      • Then she throws \(N\) frosting pieces. Due to magical gravity, the frostings fall uniformly at random on the surface of the donut (the annulus).
      • Natasha gives you the Cartesian coordinates of the frostings. Your task is to sort them by their distance from the center of the donut, from nearest to farthest.
      • If two frostings have the same distance, sort them by \(x\), then by \(y\).
    • Input:
      • The first line contains three integers \(N\) (\(1 \le N \le 10^5\)), \(R_1\), and \(R_2\) (\(1 \le R_1 < R_2 \le 10^9\)) — representing the number of frostings, the inner radius, and the outer radius, respectively.
      • Each of the following \(N\) lines contains \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) (\(R_1^2 \le X_i^2 + Y_i^2 \le R_2^2\)) — representing the coordinates of the \(i\)-th frosting.
      • It is guaranteed that all points are unique and lie inside the annulus.
    • Output:
      • Print the \(N\) points, one point per line, after sorting them in the following format:
      • \(X_1\) \(Y_1\)
      • \(X_2\) \(Y_2\)
      • : :
      • : :
      • \(X_N\) \(Y_N\)
    • Example:
      • input (Скопировать) 4 5 7 0 -6 5 0 -7 0 0 5
      • output (Скопировать) 0 5 5 0 0 -6 -7 0
    • Note:
      • In the first test case, frostings distribution can be visualized as in the following picture:

Отмечены четыре точки (кусочки глазури): 1. Фиолетовая точка вверху на оси Y: \((0, 5)\). 2. Зеленая точка справа на оси X: \((5, 0)\). 3. Оранжевая точка внизу на оси Y: \((0, -6)\). 4.     File 2: B. Cormen-Adabra

    Page 1

    System Interface & Sidebar: (Идентично File 1) * User: p0dyakov | Группы: IU DSA Spring 2026 | Topic 4. Coding exercises | Соревнование идет (4 дня).

    Problem Content: * Tab Menu: ЗАДАЧИ | ОТОСЛАТЬ | МОИ ПОСЫЛКИ | ЗАРЕГИСТРИРОВАННЫЕ УЧАСТНИКИ | ЗАПУСК * Title: B. Cormen-Adabra * Constraints: * time limit per test: 2 seconds * memory limit per test: 256 megabytes

    • Description:
      • A wizard’s spellbook (Cormen-Adabra) contains \(N\) distinct words, each assigned a unique index from \(1\) to \(N\).
      • A spell is written as a sequence of numbers, where each number represents a word from the spellbook.
      • To prevent spells from being misused, spells are stored in arbitrary order.
      • In order to apply the spells, your task is to sort them in lexicographical order based on the strings obtained by concatenating the words they represent.
    • Input:
      • The first line contains two integers \(N\) and \(M\) (\(1 \le N, M \le 10^4\)) — the number of words and the number of spells, respectively.
      • The second line contains \(N\) distinct words \(word_1, word_2, \dots, word_N\) separated by spaces, where each word consists of lower case English letters and (\(1 \le |word_i| \le 20\)).
      • Each of the following \(M\) lines describes one spell:
      • An integer \(K\) (\(1 \le K \le 10\)) — the size of the \(j\)-th spell.
      • Followed by \(K\) integers representing the \(j\)-th spell.
      • After concatenating the words corresponding to each spell, all resulting strings are guaranteed to be unique.
    • Output:
      • Print the spells in lexicographical order, using the same format as in the input.
    • Example:
      • input (Скопировать) 15 3 doing work great the are good things keep you and come up from perseverance hard 4 9 5 1 3 5 8 12 4 6 2 8 3 7 11 13 15 2 10 14
      • output (Скопировать) 8 3 7 11 13 15 2 10 14 5 8 12 4 6 2 4 9 5 1 3
    • Note:
      • In the first test case:
      • The first spell consists of the 9th, 5th, 1st, and 3rd words.
      • the second spell consists of the 8th, 12th, 4th, 6th, and 2nd words.
      • the third spell consists of the 3rd, 7th, 11th, 13th, 15th, 2nd, 10th, and 14th words.
      • After concatenating the spells we get:
      • \(\text{\color{red}you\color{blue}are\color{black}doing\color{green}great}\)
